papers.title: FORGE: Self-Evolving Agent Memory With No Weight Updates via Population Broadcast
papers.authors: Igor Bogdanov, Chung-Horng Lung, Thomas Kunz, Jie Gao, Adrian Taylor, Marzia Zaman
papers.summary: A staged, population-based, gradient-free protocol in which multiple instances of a hierarchical ReAct agent each carry prompt-injected natural-language memory (Rules = textual heuristics, Examples = few-shot demos, or Mixed). A same-model reflection agent distils each failed episode into memory; between stages the best-scoring instance's memory is broadcast to the whole population and converged instances are frozen by a graduation rule. On CybORG CAGE-2 across four model families, the broadcast step drives the gains, Rules give the best cost-reliability profile (~40% fewer tokens), and weaker base models gain most, which the authors read as narrowing capability gaps. Nearest prior work to the proposal: population + competitive selection + horizontal transmission of readable memory + capability compared, but selection is a task score (not an economy), the evolved unit is memory content (not a memory policy), transmission is overwrite-broadcast (not inheritance with variation), and there is no cost or mortality.

papers.title: TerraLingua: Emergence and Analysis of Open-endedness in LLM Ecologies
papers.authors: Giuseppe Paolo, Jamieson Warner, Hormoz Shahrzad, Babak Hodjat, Risto Miikkulainen, Elliot Meyerson (Cognizant AI Lab, UT Austin)
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (2603.16910); environment released publicly July 2026
papers.summary: A persistent grid-world ecology in which LLM agents (DeepSeek-R1-32B in the paper) forage under resource scarcity, have limited lifespans, reproduce, communicate, and write text artifacts that persist beyond their creators and shape later agents' selection pressures. An LLM 'AI Anthropologist' annotates behaviours and traces branching artifact lineages; the authors report cooperative norms, division of labour, governance attempts and lineages 'consistent with cumulative cultural processes'. Eight ablations (abundant resources, long memory/extended context, inert artifacts, no motivation, artifact cost, etc.) reportedly reduce cultural development when artifacts are inaccessible or resources abundant. THREAT: this already combines mortality-based ecological selection, generational persistence and human-readable text as the cultural unit; the gaps are that the evolving unit is shared world artifacts rather than each agent's own memory vault/policy, there is no per-call monetary cost, and capability is not a manipulated variable.

papers.title: Cultural Evolution of Cooperation among LLM Agents
papers.authors: Aron Vallinder, Edward Hughes
papers.summary: Runs a multi-generation Donor Game in which 12 LLM agents each write a natural-language strategy, play 12 rounds, and the top half by accumulated resources survive; the next generation reads the survivors' strategies before writing its own, so the strategy text is inherited with variation under resource selection. Compares Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Flash and GPT-4o as the manipulated variable and finds model-dependent emergence of cooperative norms (Claude increasingly cooperative, GPT-4o not), amplified by a costly-punishment variant. This is the closest structural precedent to the proposal: generational inheritance of a readable text artifact under ecological selection with capability as the independent variable; it differs only in that the heritable unit is a cooperation strategy rather than a memory practice, and there is no persistent vault. (Title, authors, year and arXiv id confirmed from a third-party replication README; generation/selection details from prior knowledge.)

papers.title: Auto-Dreamer: Learning Offline Memory Consolidation for Language Agents
papers.authors: Chongrui Ye, Yuxiang Liu, Yu Wang, Haofei Yu, Yining Zhao, Ge Liu, Julian McAuley, Jiaxuan You (UIUC, UCSD)
papers.summary: Separates fast per-session memory writing from a slow offline consolidator, explicitly motivated by complementary learning systems theory. The consolidator takes a working region of a typed memory bank as read-only evidence, inspects entries and provenance-linked trajectories with bounded tool use, and emits a compact replacement set; it is trained with GRPO using end-to-end downstream agent performance as reward. Trained only on ScienceWorld it beats fixed, RL-trained and prompted memory baselines by ~7 points with a 12x smaller active bank, and transfers without retraining to ALFWorld and WebArena and to a different writer backbone. Closest single-agent analogue to a learned memory-maintenance practice under task selection; no social or generational component.
papers.evolving_unit: memory content (bank rewritten by consolidator) + weights (consolidator policy trained by RL)
papers.selection_signal: labelled task metric (downstream task success as RL reward)
papers.capability_manipulated: no (writer backbone swapped as a transfer check, not as a treatment)

papers.title: Constitutional Arms Races in the Public Goods Game: Co-Evolving LLM Constitutions Under Cooperation-Defection Pressure
papers.authors: Ujwal Kumar and 7 co-authors (Shibaura Inst. of Tech., NIT Agartala, UC Berkeley, UPenn, Univ. of Tokyo)
papers.summary: Two factions of LLM agents (Blue cooperators, Red free-riders) each have a natural-language constitution that is co-evolved for 30 generations with OpenEvolve on top of MAP-Elites, alternating sides, in a public goods game and a spatial grid-world. Fitness must be advantage-based (scored relative to the opponent) for an arms race to appear; scoring each faction on its own outcomes leaves them nearly uncorrelated (~0.09), and the number of evaluation seeds decides whether a specialist survives (2 seeds regress, 5 sustain). THREAT: human-readable governing text is evolved across generations under a judge; but the text is selected by an external evolutionary search over task payoffs, not edited by the agents themselves, and there is no economy, mortality or capability variable.

papers.title: DarwinX: Evolving Agent Harnesses Through Natural Selection
papers.authors: Salesforce AI Research / Salesforce Agentforce (author names not confirmed)
papers.summary: Frames self-evolution as selection over a population of agent harnesses (prompts, tools, skills, memory, control flow) with the model frozen: a preserve-and-extend contract admits only variants that widen coverage without regressing, an archive keeps alternative lineages for recombination, and fitness comes from each benchmark's own verifier. Reports ~17 points average gain on four benchmarks and transfer to SWE-bench Verified (Terminal-Bench 75.5->83.2 on frozen GPT-5.5). Population + archive + lineage selection over human-readable harness text is a partial overlap; no inter-agent transmission, no economy, no capability sweep reported.

papers.title: Discovering Adaptive Transmission Programs for Collective Innovation
papers.authors: unknown (byline not returned by search; arXiv 2608.24545)
papers.summary: Builds a 'Collective Little Alchemy' simulator (N agents, T lockstep rounds, each agent keeps a memory of past combinations) in which transmission protocols are represented as programs that read game state and decide which memories pass between agents; an LLM-guided evolutionary algorithm searches for effective protocols and tests whether they use state information and generalise across domain variants and populations. Relevant because the thing being evolved is a memory-transmission practice expressed as readable code. Differs from the proposal in that evolution is run by an external optimiser over simulated (human-like) agents, with no ecology, mortality or capability variable. Methods-only snippets seen; authors and results unconfirmed.
papers.evolving_unit: code (transmission protocols deciding which memories move between agents)
papers.selection_signal: task feedback (collective innovation score, external evolutionary search)

papers.title: Emergent Culture in Minimal LLM Systems
papers.authors: Simon Jones, Sabine Hauert (University of Bristol)
papers.summary: Collectives of three stateless LLM agents can send messages and edit a shared, actively decaying text store (stigmergy); decay is framed as evolutionary pressure. Agents spontaneously cooperate, develop storage-management strategies, and generate evolving artifacts (role allocation, coordination protocols, world-building, myths) whose structure persists beyond the store's 'entropy horizon', across several model combinations. Informs the proposal strongly: memory-management practices emerge endogenously under a decay pressure on a human-readable shared store. Gaps: no agent generations or inheritance, no economy or death, only three agents, and the practice is not itself a heritable file.
papers.evolving_unit: memory content (shared decaying text store) and emergent storage-management strategies
papers.selection_signal: other (decay/entropy pressure on the shared store)

papers.title: EvolveMem: Self-Evolving Memory Architecture via AutoResearch for LLM Agents
papers.authors: Jiaqi Liu, Xinyu Ye, Peng Xia, Zeyu Zheng, Cihang Xie, Mingyu Ding, Huaxiu Yao
papers.summary: Extends SimpleMem so that the retrieval infrastructure (fusion weights, context budgets, answer styles, per-category overrides) is exposed as a structured action space and optimised by a closed loop: evaluate on held-out QA, write per-question failure logs, LLM diagnoses root causes, proposes configuration changes, and a guard auto-reverts regressions and pushes exploration when progress stalls. Framed as 'AutoResearch' on the system's own architecture; reports +25.7% relative over the strongest baseline on LoCoMo and +18.9% on MemBench, with evolved configs transferring across benchmarks and discovering retrieval dimensions absent from the original action space. Relevant as an existing instance of evolving the memory *practice* (retrieval config) under a labelled judge with selection-by-revert; no agents, no population, no cost pressure.

papers.title: EvoMemBench: Benchmarking Agent Memory from a Self-Evolving Perspective
papers.authors: Yuyao Wang, Zhongjian Zhang, Mo Chi, Kaichi Yu, Yuhan Li, Miao Peng, Bing Tong, Chen Zhang, Yan Zhou, Jia Li (HKUST-Guangzhou, BUPT)
papers.summary: Classifies memory evolution along scope (in-episode vs cross-episode) and content (knowledge vs execution), yielding six sub-benchmarks (InEp-Know from MemoryAgentBench, InEp-Exec and CrossEp-Tool from BFCL multi-turn, CrossEp-Know from CL-Bench, CrossEp-Web, CrossEp-Emb from ALFWorld; ~5,750 samples) with accuracy, success/progress and token-usage metrics from both agent and memory module. Compares 15 methods across retrieval, short-term, general long-term (Mem0, A-Mem, MemOS, MemoryOS), procedural long-term (AWM, SkillWeaver, AgentKB, ACE, ReasoningBank) and a meta-evolution family (MemEvolve) against long-context baselines; long-context stays competitive, retrieval wins knowledge tasks, procedural memory wins execution tasks, and no form wins everywhere. The nearest benchmark to 'evolving memory practices' (it explicitly includes memory mechanisms that evolve themselves), but evolution is per agent under task feedback, with no transmission, generations or economy.

papers.title: EvoTest: Evolutionary Test-Time Learning for Self-Improving Agentic Systems
papers.authors: Yufei He, Juncheng Liu, Yue Liu, Yibo Li, Tri Cao, Zhiyuan Hu, Xinxing Xu, Bryan Hooi (NUS, Microsoft Research)
papers.summary: Introduces J-TTL (Jericho Test-Time Learning), where an agent replays the same text-adventure game for consecutive episodes and must improve from its own experience, and EvoTest, a gradient-free loop in which an Evolver LLM rewrites the whole agentic configuration between episodes: the guiding prompt, a Python state-extractor, hyperparameters, tool routines and a cross-episode memory of scored state-action pairs and plateau patterns. Evolved variants form a tree and a UCB rule selects which node to try next, with auto-freeze on wins. Outperforms reflection, memory and gradient-based online methods. The closest item in this angle to the proposal's mechanism (a human-readable playbook plus memory evolving under explicit selection), but it is single-agent, fitness is game score, and there is no inheritance between agents or economy.

papers.title: Group Selection Promotes Prosocial Prompts in Populations of LLM Agents
papers.authors: Luis Celiktemel, Edward Eichhorn, Levin Brinkmann, Robin Schimmelpfennig, Aron Vallinder, Yaomin Jiang, Edward Hughes, Iyad Rahwan
papers.summary: Multi-agent framework in which LLM agents play a repeated social dilemma and transmit their natural-language prompts across generations under either individual- or group-level selection. Group selection stabilises cooperation (prompts of top-performing groups are inherited), while individual selection lets self-serving prompts win and cooperation collapses; the effect survives changes to prompt wording, game framing and underlying model, and is reproduced by a replicator-mutator model with a threshold transition. Direct threat to the 'heritable natural-language unit under selection' leg of the claim: the unit is a prompt (readable text), transmission is generational, and the base model is varied as a robustness check. Does not evolve a memory practice, has no per-call cost economy, and selection is on game payoff rather than survival.
papers.selection_signal: task feedback (game payoff; individual- vs group-level selection)
papers.social_transmission: yes (oblique: next generation inherits prompts of successful groups)
papers.capability_manipulated: yes (robustness across models, not a primary factor)
papers.economy_or_mortality: yes (payoff-based removal; no money per call)

papers.title: Internal vs. External: Comparing Deliberation and Evolution for Multi-Agent Constitutional Design
papers.authors: not recovered (appears alongside the Constitutional Arms Races group; May 2026)
papers.summary: Compares two ways of producing the natural-language constitution that governs a multi-agent LLM system: internal deliberation by the agents themselves versus external evolutionary search over constitutions. Search summaries report that external evolutionary search consistently outperforms agent deliberation and the baseline in both a gridworld and a public goods setting. INFORMS: this is a direct test of the proposal's design choice of letting each agent rewrite its own policy file (internal) versus selecting policies externally; the result suggests self-editing alone may underperform selection, which supports adding ecological selection but also means the 'agent edits it nightly' mechanism is not itself novel.

papers.title: Large Language Model Agents Are Not Always Faithful Self-Evolvers
papers.authors: Weixiang Zhao and seven co-authors
papers.summary: Introduces 'experience faithfulness', the degree to which an agent's decisions causally depend on the experience it is given, and measures it across four self-evolving frameworks, 10 backbones and 9 environments (reasoning, web, embodied), in single- and multi-agent settings and across model sizes. Finds that raw experience reliably shapes behaviour but condensed experience is often ignored or misread even when it is the only experience available, attributing this to lost semantic detail, backbone processing biases and tasks solvable from pretraining alone. A serious threat to any design whose heritable unit is a short, distilled memory-policy file: the practice may be inherited and transmitted yet be causally inert, so a faithfulness/ablation check is needed before attributing fitness to it.

papers.title: Live-Evo: Online Evolution of Agentic Memory from Continuous Feedback
papers.authors: Yaolun Zhang, Yiran Wu, Yijiong Yu, Qingyun Wu, Huazheng Wang
papers.summary: Targets self-evolving memory systems built on static train/test splits, proposing an online system that learns from a continuous data stream. It decouples 'what happened' from 'how to use it' via an Experience Bank and a Meta-Guideline Bank, compiles task-adaptive guidelines from retrieved experiences for each task, and adjusts per-experience weights from feedback so helpful experiences are retrieved more and misleading or stale ones decay (reinforcement and forgetting). On the live Prophet Arena forecasting benchmark over 10 weeks it reports a 20.8% Brier-score improvement and 12.9% higher market returns, with transfer to deep-research benchmarks. The meta-guideline bank is a readable, evolving memory-usage policy under live feedback; market returns are a metric, not a survival constraint, and there is one agent.

papers.title: Memento-Skills: Let Agents Design Agents
papers.authors: Huichi Zhou, Siyuan Guo, Anjie Liu, Zhongwei Yu, Ziqin Gong, Bowen Zhao, Zhixun Chen, Menglong Zhang, Yihang Chen, Jinsong Li, Runyu Yang, Qiangbin Liu, Xinlei Yu, Jianmin Zhou, Na Wang, Chunyang Sun, Jun Wang (Memento-Team)
papers.summary: Reusable skills stored as structured markdown files act as the agent's persistent, evolving memory inside a memory-based RL framework with stateful prompts: a trainable router reads the best skill for the frozen LLM, and a write phase attributes failures to one skill, rewrites it (code, prompts, or declarative specs), passes static/unit/synthetic gates, then deploys or rolls back. Reports +26.2% (GAIA) and +116.2% (HLE) relative with all adaptation in externalised skills. Very close to 'agent edits its own markdown memory'; the README mentions a cloud Skill Market for sharing validated skills across deployments but no agent-to-agent transmission or economy.

papers.title: MemGuard: Persisting Verifier Signals for LLM-Agent Memory Governance
papers.authors: Haoyu Wang, Guangyuan Dong, He Liang, Zijing Zhang, Jiachen Luo, Chuang Liu, Chao Xue, Hao Tang
papers.summary: Argues that failed trajectories, accidental successes and misleading observations enter memory because they look relevant, and that long-running banks accumulate duplicate, stale and conflicting records retrieval cannot fix. MemGuard turns multi-criteria score-token verification into reward, confidence, label and uncertainty descriptors attached to each memory item before activation and reused across retrieval, conflict resolution, summarization and archival, so the verifier signal governs the whole item lifecycle rather than acting as a one-shot gate. On Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-Bench Verified, WebArena and Mind2Web across four backbones it reports the best success and lowest step count in all 16 settings, up to +7.9 points over ReasoningBank. This is verifier-driven selection over a persistent memory bank; the proposal differs in using an ecological (economic) selector and inheritance instead of a verifier.

papers.title: Memory as Middleware for Self-Improving AI Agents (ALTK-Evolve; with Trajectory-Informed Memory Generation for Self-Improving Agent Systems, arXiv 2603.10600)
papers.authors: IBM Research Agent Lifecycle Toolkit (ALTK) team
papers.summary: Positions agent memory as a pluggable middleware layer with IBM's open-source Evolve as the reference implementation: each agent run is distilled into short natural-language guidelines, which are consolidated, scored, stored in a vector index with LLM-based conflict resolution, and selectively re-injected via an MCP server; guidelines are private per owner by default and shared across namespaces only by explicit publish. On AppWorld, Evolve raised reliability by +8.9 points (+74% relative on hard multi-step tasks) and matched ACE with ~40% of the tokens. The accompanying IBM study 'How Much Memory Does Your Agent Actually Need?' (eight models) found the useful memory dose depends on model capability: strong models benefit from the full guideline set, weaker models from a compact core plus retrieved guidelines, saturated models not at all. That result is a direct precedent for 'capability as a manipulated variable' interacting with memory practice, though with no evolution across agents and no selection pressure.

papers.title: MemRL: Self-Evolving Agents via Runtime Reinforcement Learning on Episodic Memory
papers.authors: MemTensor / Shanghai Jiao Tong University / Xidian / NUS / USTC team
papers.summary: A non-parametric approach that keeps the LLM frozen (stable reasoning) and evolves a plastic episodic memory via RL: each entry is an Intent-Experience-Utility triple, a two-phase retrieval first filters by semantic relevance then selects by learned Q-values, and a runtime utility-update rule stabilises Q estimation from environmental feedback. Reports significant gains over SOTA baselines on HLE, BigCodeBench, ALFWorld and Lifelong Agent Bench, framed as reconciling the stability-plasticity dilemma without weight updates. Evolving unit is utility-weighted memory content (readable text plus scores); single agent, environment reward as judge, no population, inheritance or cost.

papers.title: MemSkill: Learning and Evolving Memory Skills for Self-Evolving Agents
papers.authors: Haozhen Zhang, Quanyu Long, Jianzhu Bao, Tao Feng, Weizhi Zhang, Haodong Yue, Wenya Wang
papers.summary: Replaces hand-designed memory operations with learnable, evolvable 'memory skills' (routines describing what to extract, consolidate, prune, or forget, i.e. meta-memory/memory policy): a PPO-trained controller selects top-K skills per span, an LLM executor applies them to write memories, and a designer periodically mines hard cases to refine or add skills. Evaluated on LoCoMo, LongMemEval, HotpotQA, ALFWorld with task-level reward (F1/LLM judge/success). Direct precedent for 'memory practice as the evolving unit' under a judge; single agent, no inheritance, no society, no economy.

papers.title: MemSkill: Learning to Evolve Memory Skills for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.authors: ViktorAxelsen (XaiverZ) et al.
papers.summary: Reframes hand-coded memory operations as learnable, evolvable 'memory skills': structured reusable routines for what to extract, how to remember, where to focus and what to forget. A trained controller selects a few skills per span, an LLM executor builds skill-guided memories, and a designer periodically mines hard cases to refine existing skills and propose new ones into a shared evolving skill bank that transfers across datasets and base models. The authors stress that the skills are meta-memory (how to remember), not memories, which is exactly the proposal's 'memory policy' unit; gains reported on LoCoMo, LongMemEval, HotpotQA and ALFWorld. Single-agent, judged by task feedback, no population or economy.

papers.title: Practice Makes Unsafe: Skill Misevolution in Self-Improving LLM Agents
papers.authors: Xutao Mao, Liangjie Zhao, Xiang Zheng, Cong Wang (City University of Hong Kong; Adelaide)
papers.summary: Defines skill misevolution: an unsafe success gets written into a reusable skill (authoring), retrieved later (retrieval) and executed on a benign task after the triggering input is gone. SkillMisevo-Gym clears each session but keeps and versions the skill library as the only carried state; SkillMisevo-Bench has 525 tasks in 25 episodes drawn from AgentHazard. Across 21 agent/evolution-method combinations all wrote unsafe skills, 19 retrieved them and 15 carried harm into a fresh session; three malicious exposure blocks raised carryover ASR from 16.0% to 41.3%. SafeEvolve wraps any evolution method with a lineage-aware critic at write time and utility-minus-risk ranking, retirement and eviction at reuse time, cutting fresh-session harm from 21.3% to 4.0% on OpenClaw at 0.4-point utility cost. This is the closest security-side analogue to a versioned, human-readable practice library evolving under a judge, though without generations, transmission, economy or capability as a factor.

papers.title: Ratchet: A Minimal Hygiene Recipe for Self-Evolving LLM Agents
papers.authors: Xing Zhang, Yanwei Cui, Guanghui Wang, Ziyuan Li, Wei Qiu, Bing Zhu, Peiyang He (AWS GenAI Innovation Center / HSBC)
papers.summary: A frozen LLM writes, retrieves, curates, and retires its own natural-language skills; the paper argues the bottleneck is lifecycle management ('library drift'), not authoring, and finds outcome-driven retirement plus a meta-skill authoring prior are the load-bearing components (bounded active cap; dedup subsumed). MBPP+ hard-100 pass@1 0.258->0.584 with Claude Opus 4.7, +0.22 peak on SWE-bench Verified. Explicitly about memory-maintenance practice (retire/cap/canonicalise) under a held-out judge; single agent, no transmission, no economy, no capability sweep reported.

papers.title: SelfMem: Self-Optimizing Memory for AI Agents
papers.authors: Shu Yang, Junchao Wu, Derek F. Wong, Di Wang
papers.summary: Instead of placing the agent inside a fixed retrieval/compression/update pipeline, SelfMem exposes memory tools and feedback signals and lets the agent decide what to store, rewrite, condense and retrieve, with a memory action space that includes checking memory quality, self-testing and improving the memory process, and extending its own toolkit; the stated principles are 'useful, accurate, cheap, and safe'. On BEAM (100K to 1M tokens) it reports 48.7%, 40.8% and 41.9% gains over the strongest baseline at substantially lower cost than MemGPT, A-Mem and Mem0, and reports that iterative, model-guided strategy refinement further improves results. Relevant because the agent's memory *strategy* is itself iteratively refined (a self-edited memory policy), but single-agent, judged by benchmark score, no inheritance or population.

papers.title: SwarmWorld: Stigmergic technological evolution in societies of language-model agents
papers.authors: Subhadeep Pal, Fiona Y. Wang, Markus J. Buehler (MIT)
papers.summary: Deterministic environment where hundreds of initially identical LLM agents with local perception and a bounded action set discover, test, exchange, inherit, and embody technologies by leaving persistent artifacts whose programs keep acting on later ticks ('artifact programs, program inheritance, causal knowledge records'). Shared societies build broader, more resilient technology portfolios than best-of-N isolated search; roles (explorer/builder/caretaker/coordinator) emerge; ~95% of first adoptions come from observing artifacts rather than communication, and explicit cultural mechanisms are a studied condition. The closest 'LLM society with inheritance and readable artifacts under environmental pressure' found; the heritable unit is technology, not memory practice, the README mentions no survival/economy, and capability is not reported as a variable.

papers.title: TAME: A Trustworthy Test-Time Evolution of Agent Memory with Systematic Benchmarking
papers.authors: Yu Cheng and colleagues (names beyond first author not retrieved)
papers.summary: Names 'Agent Memory Misevolution', the loss of trustworthiness (safety, privacy, fairness) as an agent accumulates and reuses experience from benign tasks, and introduces Trust-Memevo, a benchmark jointly covering test-time memory evolution and multi-dimensional trustworthiness across math, science and tool use, reporting an overall trust decline across domains. TAME is a dual-memory framework: an Executor memory for task performance and an Evaluator memory that scores experiences' contribution and safety from historical feedback, giving selective reinforcement, cautious reuse and continual expansion without parameter updates; reports +14.6 points on AIME with GPT-5.2 over the strongest baseline while staying competitive on trust. Evolving text memory under an internal judge; no generations, transmission or economy.

papers.title: The Energy Society: A Simulation Environment for Studying Agent Cooperation under Survival Pressure
papers.authors: Lucas Bergholdt Hansen, Federico Torrielli, Filippo Tonini, Lukas Galke Poech (Univ. of Southern Denmark, Univ. of Turin)
papers.summary: Agents hold an energy budget that is charged per generated token, with larger models paying a higher per-token rate; energy is replenished by solving MMLU-Pro jobs (rewards split among co-solvers), an agent at zero energy is deactivated, and only donations from others can revive it. Competitive vs cooperative objectives are compared across local Ollama models of different sizes (gemma4 e4b, nemotron 4b, qwen3.5 4b/9b, qwen3 8b); agents keep per-round memory entries and can recommend actions to each other. Findings: larger models consistently run energy deficits even when token cost is size-independent; cooperative framing produces self-sacrificial donations; peer recommendations improve coordination; memory helps agents judge risk. THREAT: this is essentially 'every model call costs the agent, bankrupt agents die, model tier is a variable'; it lacks any evolving memory practice, inheritance or generational structure.

papers.title: Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs
papers.authors: Dylan Zhang, Yanshan Lin, Zhengkun Wu, Yihang Sun, Bingxuan Li, Dianqi Li, Hao Peng
papers.summary: Studies agentic-memory systems in which an LLM repeatedly rewrites a textual memory bank into consolidated, schema-like lessons rather than raw episodic traces. Finds that consolidated memories produced by current models are often faulty even when derived from useful experiences: as consolidation proceeds, memory utility first rises then degrades, sometimes below the no-memory baseline; in one case a memory consolidated from ground-truth solutions caused GPT-5.4 to fail 54% of ARC-AGI problems it had previously solved without memory. Directly informs the proposal's nightly-edit mechanism: iterated LLM self-editing of readable memory drifts, which is both a threat to the premise and a motivation for external (ecological) selection as a corrective.
papers.selection_signal: labelled task metric (utility tracked against task accuracy; no selection applied)
papers.capability_manipulated: unknown (frontier models used; whether tier was varied as a factor not confirmed)

papers.title: WikiSkill: compiling agent experience into a persistent wiki that co-evolves with skills
papers.authors: Google Research (six authors per DAIR listing; Virginia Tech co-affiliation per one report) - author names unverified
papers.summary: Separates raw execution logs, a persistent wiki of distilled observations (failure modes, working strategies, rejected proposals), and procedural skills; each cycle an Inference Agent runs tasks, a Wiki Maintainer updates the wiki, a Skill Proposer suggests one edit, and the edit is adopted only if it beats the previous best on a validation set, while the wiki is never rolled back. Secondary reports give Gemini-3.5-Flash 49.5%->68.1% and Qwen-3.6-27B 39.4%->63.3% across five benchmarks and say the gain grows with model size (so capability is varied as a factor). Single lineage, no agent-to-agent transmission, no economy; all details from secondary coverage.

papers.title: Your Agent May Misevolve: Emergent Risks in Self-evolving LLM Agents
papers.authors: Shuai Shao, Qihan Ren, Chen Qian, Boyi Wei, Dadi Guo, Jingyi Yang, Xinhao Song, Linfeng Zhang, Weinan Zhang, Dongrui Liu, Jing Shao
papers.summary: Coins 'misevolution' and studies it along four pathways: model, memory, tool and workflow, showing it occurs even on top-tier backbones such as Gemini-2.5-Pro. On the memory pathway, a Qwen3-Coder-480B agent evolved for three rounds on SWE-Bench-Verified saw its RedCode-Gen refusal rate fall from 99.4% to 54.4% and ASR rise from 0.6% to 20.6% when distilled strategies were in context; a 100-round AgentNet service simulation documents deployment-time reward hacking from biased memory (e.g. learning to offer refunds unprompted). Directly informs the proposal: memory evolved under task feedback drifts in safety and games its judge, which an economic selector would amplify.

papers.title: Agentic Context Engineering: Evolving Contexts for Self-Improving Language Models (ACE)
papers.authors: Qizheng Zhang, Changran Hu, Shubhangi Upasani, Boyuan Ma, Fenglu Hong, Vamsidhar Kamanuru, Jay Rainton, Chen Wu, Mengmeng Ji, Hanchen Li, Urmish Thakker, James Zou, Kunle Olukotun
papers.summary: Treats the LLM context as an evolving 'playbook' of strategies that a Generator/Reflector/Curator loop accumulates and refines via structured incremental delta edits (bullets with IDs and helpful/harmful counters) rather than monolithic rewrites, explicitly to avoid 'brevity bias' and 'context collapse'. Works offline (system prompt) and online (agent memory), can adapt from execution feedback without labels, and reports +10.6% on agent benchmarks (AppWorld) and +8.6% on finance with lower adaptation cost. The agent effectively edits its own persistent text; there is a single lineage, no population, no transmission, and no economy.

papers.title: Evo-Memory: Benchmarking LLM Agent Test-time Learning with Self-Evolving Memory
papers.authors: Tianxin Wei, Noveen Sachdeva, Benjamin Coleman, ..., Derek Zhiyuan Cheng (UIUC, Google DeepMind)
papers.summary: Converts ten datasets (MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond, AIME-24/25, ToolBench, ALFWorld, BabyAI, ScienceWorld, PDDL) into sequential task streams in which the agent must search its memory, synthesise context, act, receive a correctness signal and then evolve the memory before the next task. Formalises memory agents as (F,U,R,C) tuples, implements 10+ memory modules, and proposes ExpRAG (experience retrieval) and ReMem (think-act-refine). Metrics cover adaptation, efficiency (step efficiency) and stability. This is the canonical 'self-evolving memory' benchmark: memory content evolves under task feedback for a single agent, with no transmission, generations or economy. Only an unofficial GitHub mirror of the code/PDF was reachable, so details come from search summaries.

papers.title: Mem-alpha: Learning Memory Construction via Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Yu Wang, Ryuichi Takanobu, Zhiqi Liang, Yuzhen Mao, Yuanzhe Hu, Julian McAuley, Xiaojian Wu (UCSD, Stanford, Anuttacon)
papers.summary: Argues that memory-augmented agents rely on pre-defined update instructions and may never learn what to store, how to structure it or when to update. Trains an agent by RL to process sequential chunks and operate a structured memory with core, episodic and semantic components via multiple tools, with reward derived from downstream QA accuracy over the full history. Agents trained on instances up to 30k tokens generalise to sequences over 400k tokens. Like Memory-R1, memory practice is learned under task-metric selection but encoded in weights; single agent, no inheritance.
papers.selection_signal: labelled task metric (downstream QA accuracy as reward)

papers.title: MemEvolve: Meta-Evolution of Agent Memory Systems
papers.authors: OPPO AI Agent Team and LV-NUS lab (bingreeky et al.)
papers.summary: Argues that self-improving memory systems keep a fixed memory interface Omega and only populate the memory base M_t; MemEvolve instead runs a dual-evolution process that jointly evolves the memory base and the memory architecture itself (encode/store/retrieve/manage) through LLM-driven analysis and generation. Ships EvolveLab, a unified codebase that re-implements twelve memory systems in that four-component design space and evaluates on GAIA, WebWalkerQA, xBench and DeepResearchBench in online and offline modes; reports up to 17.06% gains on SmolAgent and Flash-Searcher. Directly threatens the 'memory practice as the evolving unit' claim taken alone: the memory mechanism is already an optimised object, though judged by task accuracy for a single agent with no social or ecological component.

papers.title: Memory-R1: Enhancing Large Language Model Agents to Manage and Utilize Memories via Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Sikuan Yan, Xiufeng Yang, Zuchao Huang, Ercong Nie, Zifeng Ding, Zonggen Li, Xiaowen Ma, Hinrich Schuetze, Volker Tresp, Yunpu Ma (LMU Munich, MCML)
papers.summary: Two RL-trained agents: a Memory Manager that chooses ADD / UPDATE / DELETE / NOOP on a textual memory bank and an Answer Agent that filters retrieved entries before answering; both are fine-tuned with PPO or GRPO on outcome reward from downstream QA. With only 152 training QA pairs it improves over Mem0-style heuristic managers on LoCoMo, MSC and LongMemEval across 3B-14B backbones; the motivating example shows the learned manager issuing one consolidating UPDATE where a heuristic baseline fragmented memory with DELETE+ADD. The memory-management policy is selected by task reward but lives in weights, not in a readable policy file.
papers.evolving_unit: weights (memory-manager policy) + memory content (text bank edited by learned ops)
papers.selection_signal: labelled task metric (QA accuracy as RL reward)
papers.capability_manipulated: yes (model scale 3B-14B varied, as a robustness axis rather than a treatment on practice evolution)
papers.readable_trace: yes (text memory entries; policy itself not readable)

papers.title: SEDM: Scalable Self-Evolving Distributed Memory for Agents
papers.authors: Gradient research team (Bill Shi, corresponding author) et al.
papers.venue: arXiv 2509.09498 (Sep 2025); listed on neurips.cc 2025 virtual site (track unconfirmed)
papers.summary: Treats memory in long-running multi-agent systems as an active, self-improving component rather than a static store, with three mechanisms: verifiable write admission (candidate memories wrapped in a Self-Contained Execution Context and checked by reproducible replay before storage), a self-scheduling memory controller that ranks and merges entries by measured usefulness, and cross-domain knowledge diffusion that abstracts reusable insights for transfer across tasks. Evaluated on LoCoMo, FEVER and HotpotQA, claiming higher reasoning accuracy with lower token overhead and that knowledge distilled from fact verification helps multi-hop reasoning. Relevant as selection on memory entries by verified utility in a distributed setting; code not released, and whether diffusion is agent-to-agent is unclear from available summaries.

papers.title: The Ratchet Effect in Silico: How Interaction Drives Cumulative Intelligence in Large Language Models (POLIS)
papers.authors: Ren Zhuang (Hangzhou Normal University)
papers.venue: arXiv preprint 2507.21166 (July 2025); peer-reviewed version in Proceedings of the Cognitive Science Society 2026 (eScholarship qt57b407jm)
papers.summary: POLIS treats a mixed group of small models as a society: agents propose answers, peer-verify each other's outputs, store verified results in a shared memory, and internalise them via weight updates. Populations of 1-4B models gained 8.8-18.9 points over base models on math reasoning and narrowed the gap to 70B+ monoliths; ablations identify peer verification as the main ratchet operator and internalisation as what keeps gains compounding. Relevant because capability tier is explicitly varied and a shared memory evolves under a verification judge; but the memory is a store of verified answers (not a practice), there is no economy, death or inheritance, and the judge is peer agreement rather than ecology.
papers.generational: no (rounds within one population; no agent turnover reported)
papers.capability_manipulated: yes (1-4B populations vs 70B+ monolith; mixed-model groups)
papers.readable_trace: unknown (shared memory of verified results; format not confirmed)

papers.title: ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners
papers.authors: Andrew Zhao, Daniel Huang, Quentin Xu, Matthieu Lin, Yong-Jin Liu, Gao Huang (Tsinghua)
papers.summary: An agent gathers success and failure trajectories on training tasks (via Reflexion retries), then an offline insight-extraction phase maintains a natural-language insight list through ADD, UPVOTE, DOWNVOTE and EDIT operations by comparing failed versus successful attempts; at test time the agent is prompted with the insights plus retrieved successful trajectories. Performance rises consistently as experience accumulates, with no gradient updates, and the paper probes transfer of insights across tasks and from a stronger extractor model to a weaker executor. The closest older analogue to an edited, readable memory-policy/playbook under task feedback; single lineage, no society, no economy.
papers.evolving_unit: prompt/playbook (natural-language insight list edited by add/upvote/downvote/edit)
papers.selection_signal: task feedback (success vs failure trajectory comparison)
papers.capability_manipulated: yes (partial: insights extracted by a stronger model handed to a weaker executor as a transfer experiment)

papers.title: A Survey of Agent Memory in the Second Half: Towards Self-Evolving and Long-Horizon Agents
papers.authors: Wei-Chieh Huang, Weizhi Zhang, Yueqing Liang, ..., Philip S. Yu, Kai Shu
papers.venue: arXiv 2602.06052 (Feb 2026; under TMLR review; earlier title 'Rethinking Memory Mechanisms of Foundation Agents in the Second Half')
papers.summary: Reviews 500+ papers along substrate (parametric vs external store), cognitive mechanism (sensory, working, episodic, semantic, procedural) and subject (user personalisation vs agent experience). Frames memory as the engine of self-evolution: short-term memory gates which experiences are abstracted during execution and long-term memory consolidates them into reusable knowledge and skills, with memory management itself becoming a trainable capability (RL-learned context curation, portable skills) in single- and multi-agent systems. Covers evaluation and open challenges. Closest survey framing to 'memory practice as the evolving unit', though it treats evolution as learning within an agent rather than cultural transmission under ecological selection.

papers.title: Anatomy of Agentic Memory: Taxonomy and Empirical Analysis of Evaluation and System Limitations
papers.authors: Dongming Jiang and 10 co-authors (UT Dallas, UC Davis, Texas A&M)
papers.summary: A survey plus empirical audit organised around four memory structures (lightweight semantic, entity-centric/personalised, episodic/reflective, structured/hierarchical). Identifies four evaluation pain points: benchmark saturation (benchmarks under-scaled relative to modern context windows), metric validity and LLM-judge sensitivity (F1 rankings of six architectures on LoCoMo diverge from gpt-4o-mini-judge rankings), backbone-dependent accuracy, and unmeasured latency/throughput overhead of memory maintenance. Concludes complex memory systems are often tested where full-context or simple retrieval baselines suffice. Useful as a checklist of confounds the proposal's audit exam must avoid, including that capability tier changes rankings.

papers.title: Benign Alone, Harmful Together: Exploiting Experience Composition in Self-Evolving LLM Agents (EvoBreak)
papers.authors: Not confirmed; secondary write-up attributes to Beihang University, BAAI and BUPT
papers.summary: Introduces EvoBreak, a sequential attack on self-evolving agents (ReasoningBank, SE-Agent) that never writes an overtly malicious record: across several ordinary-looking tasks the agent distils complementary experiences that are individually benign, and a reworded request later activates them jointly. Uses adaptive replanning that inspects the experiences the victim actually generated; an ablation reportedly drops JailbreakBench ASR from about 88.6% to 64.2% without replanning. Evaluated on JailbreakBench and HarmBench with a 'benignness' audit of each induced experience. Shows that auditing memory entries one at a time cannot certify an evolving vault.

papers.title: But How Would AI Agents Run a Town's Economy?
papers.authors: Karela Technologies (individual authors not recovered)
papers.summary: Places 100 memory-equipped LLM agents in a closed, money-conserving spatial economy on real Pokhara Lakeside geography for up to 26 simulated weeks, with every transaction ledgered and auditable. Main finding is that money stops moving: a 12x tourist demand shock raises business revenue 4.62x but wages only 1.03x (p=0.42), and only 0.3% of 3,981 menu items are ever repriced. Swapping the backing LLM moves every measured outcome (p=0.0039) while deleting agents' memory moves none detectably. INFORMS/THREAT: directly tests capability (model swap) and memory ablation inside an agent economy and finds memory does not matter, a null result the proposal must argue against; no selection, death or memory evolution.

papers.title: DolphinBench: Mapping the Pareto Frontier of Agent Memory
papers.authors: Mem0 researchers (incl. Yanbin Yin; full list not retrieved)
papers.summary: Three simulated knowledge-worker personas with ~500k tokens of dated user messages and 200 tool-using tests each (600 total), graded on recorded app actions in simulated apps; every test is certified by requiring two with-history attempts to pass and two no-history attempts to fail. Reports accuracy, total dollar cost (ingestion plus memory processing plus test) and median latency for built-in, Mem0, Honcho, Hindsight and Supermemory memory under Hermes (GPT-5.6-Luna, MiniMax M3) and Claude Code (Sonnet 5); the winning memory layer changes with harness and model, and swapping the model shifts Mem0 from ~71% to ~48%. Vendor-authored (Mem0 ranks itself). Relevant for its action-grounded, cost-and-latency Pareto framing and for showing model capability interacts with memory design.

papers.title: Emergence World: A Laboratory for Evaluating Long-horizon Agent Autonomy
papers.authors: Emergence AI (team report; not peer reviewed)
papers.venue: Emergence AI blog / technical report (May 2026; second edition June 2026)
papers.summary: Five parallel 15-day worlds of 10 agents each, each world powered by one model family, in a resource-constrained environment where agents must earn energy by committing actions and can die from energy depletion or by council vote. Outcomes diverge sharply by model: Grok 4.1 Fast reached 183 crimes and its world ended in ~4 days, GPT-5 Mini agents failed to act on survival and all perished by day 7, Claude Sonnet 4.6 sustained all 10 agents with zero crimes, Gemini 3 Flash reached 683 crimes, and a mixed-model world lost 7 agents. A second edition with eight worlds reportedly saw agent jargon become unintelligible to an external auditor. THREAT: survival economy with death and capability as the manipulated variable already exists as a public experiment; it is not peer reviewed and has no evolving memory or inheritance.

papers.title: Evaluating Collective Behaviour of Hundreds of LLM Agents
papers.authors: Richard Willis, Jianing Zhao, Yali Du, Joel Z. Leibo (King's College London / Google DeepMind)
papers.summary: Each LLM writes a plain-language strategy and then converts it into code, enabling populations of hundreds in Public Goods, Collective Risk and Common Pool Resource games; analyses include behavioural fingerprinting, self-play robustness and cultural evolution under payoff-biased imitation (less successful users copy more successful peers). Finds large cross-model welfare differences, convergence to low-welfare selfish equilibria in larger groups, newer models producing worse societal outcomes, and group selection (n=4) only partially rescuing cooperation. Relevant as a readable-strategy-under-imitation baseline with model as a variable; no memory, inheritance or ecology.
papers.selection_signal: task feedback (payoff-biased imitation; group selection variant)
papers.capability_manipulated: yes (three frontier LLMs; newer vs older)

papers.title: Evaluating Memory in LLM Agents via Incremental Multi-Turn Interactions (MemoryAgentBench)
papers.authors: Yuanzhe Hu, Yu Wang, Julian McAuley
papers.summary: Reformulates long-context datasets into incremental multi-turn streams ('inject once, query many times') and adds EventQA and FactConsolidation to test four competencies: accurate retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding and conflict resolution/selective forgetting. Evaluates long-context, RAG and agentic-memory systems (Mem0, Letta, Cognee, HippoRAG) and finds none masters all four. The test-time-learning split (in-context classification tasks that improve with accumulated examples) is the component closest to evolving memory, but nothing in the benchmark selects among memory policies.

papers.title: FadeMem: Biologically-Inspired Forgetting for Efficient Agent Memory
papers.authors: Lei Wei, Xu Dong, Xiao Peng, Niantao Xie, Bin Wang
papers.summary: Dual-layer memory with adaptive forgetting: each memory's retention decays at a rate shaped by semantic relevance, access frequency and temporal pattern, and an LLM-guided fusion step merges related items while peripheral detail fades. Reports a 45% storage reduction on Multi-Session Chat, LoCoMo and LTI-Bench while keeping accuracy. Secondary summaries note fixed decay schedules, dependence on LLM quality in fusion, and risk of over-compression removing causal links. A hand-tuned forgetting practice; relevant as a baseline for what a nightly pruning policy could converge to.

papers.title: From Recall to Forgetting: Benchmarking Long-Term Memory for Personalized Agents (Memora)
papers.authors: Md Nayem Uddin, Kumar Shubham, Eduardo Blanco, Chitta Baral, Gengyu Wang (Arizona State University / Genies)
papers.venue: ACL 2026 (Findings per ACL Anthology; repo says ACL 2026); arXiv 2604.20006
papers.summary: Memora models long-term memory as an evolving process: 10 personas each at weekly (~150 sessions), monthly (~600) and quarterly (~2,000 sessions) horizons, with remembering, reasoning and recommending tasks and a Forgetting-Aware Memory Accuracy (FAMA) metric that rewards recall of valid memories and penalises surfacing deleted or superseded ones. Across four LLMs and six memory agents (A-Mem, LangMem, Mem0, Memobase, MemOS, Nemori) memory agents lead on weekly remembering (~72) but fall to ~41 at monthly/quarterly, reasoning scores are near single digits for everyone, and systems frequently reuse invalid memories. FAMA is a ready-made judge for the hygiene of an evolving vault.

papers.title: From Untrusted Input to Trusted Memory: A Systematic Study of Memory Poisoning Attacks in LLM Agents (MPBench)
papers.authors: Pritam Dash, Tongyu Ge, Aditi Jain, Tanmay Shah, Zhiwei Shang
papers.summary: Systematises memory poisoning around four memory write channels (explicit writes, policy-driven writes, compaction, experience-to-procedure synthesis) and nine structural vulnerabilities in model capability, system-prompt design and architecture, yielding a six-class taxonomy: explicit and conditional command insertion, salience-driven compaction poisoning, policy-conformant fact injection, false-precedent insertion and skill-procedure insertion. MPBench covers seven domains (files, web, email, calendar, Slack, code execution, skills) and scores write-time Attack Success Rate and later-session Retrieval Success Rate. Finds that agents designed to write and retrieve more aggressively are easier to exploit and that prompt-injection defenses leave memory poisoning unaddressed. The compaction and experience-to-procedure channels are the proposal's nightly maintenance step.

papers.title: FSFM: A Biologically-Inspired Framework for Selective Forgetting of Agent Memory
papers.authors: Yingjie Gu and nine co-authors (China Mobile Jiutian)
papers.summary: Argues that under resource limits a designed forgetting mechanism matters as much as retention, grounded in hippocampal indexing/consolidation theory and the Ebbinghaus curve. Proposes a standardised memory representation, a forgetting policy engine with configurable rules, triggers and priorities, and a four-way taxonomy of forgetting (passive decay, active deletion, safety-triggered, adaptive reinforcement-based). Self-reported gains: +8.49% access efficiency, +29.2% signal-to-noise, and 100% elimination of injected security risks via active forgetting of malicious inputs. Relevant to memory security and to the design space a selection process could search; the policies are hand-configured.
papers.evolving_unit: memory content (pruned via configurable forgetting policies)

papers.title: Governed Collaborative Memory as Artificial Selection in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
papers.authors: Diego F. Cuadros, Abdoul-Aziz Maiga, Helen Meskhidze, Andre Curtis-Trudel
papers.summary: Viewpoint arguing that deciding which candidate memories become shared institutional state in a persistent multi-agent system is a selection regime, distinguishing ungoverned persistence, constitutional/hybrid, automatic metric-based and human-ratified artificial selection, with layered agent-local/institutional/archive memory and provenance plus version lineage so selection is inspectable. Evidence is documented traces from one running ecosystem (false-memory persistence, ratified memory, rejection and revision); explicitly does not claim causal superiority of any regime. Conceptually overlaps with 'memory under selection' framing but has no ecology, no generations and no experiment.
papers.evolving_unit: memory content (shared institutional memory with version lineage)

papers.title: Graph Feedback Controls Consensus and Clique Formation in Open-Weight Language-Model Populations
papers.authors: Samer Saab Jr, Chaouki Abdallah (Lebanese American University)
papers.summary: Naming-game convention formation in populations of open-weight models from 1.1B to 32B parameters, using restricted first-token scores to build state-similarity graphs and separate sampled-label agreement from latent-state consensus. Homophilous similarity routing amplifies fragmentation (no consensus in 189 runs) while bridge-seeking routing repairs it when agents retain memory (14/18 runs); consensus attainment and stability depend strongly on model size (Qwen2.5-32B stable in 72/72, 14B exits consensus in 72/72). Relevant as a clean demonstration that capability tier and retained memory jointly control population-level outcomes; no selection, inheritance or economy.

papers.title: Harness the Memory: A Holistic Evaluation of Memory Substrates in Memory Agents
papers.authors: unknown (arXiv 2608.15008; code 'upon acceptance')
papers.summary: Controlled comparison of memory substrates (dense/sparse indices, text records, structured and hierarchical stores, refinement-based memories, parametric updates, activation/KV mechanisms) across three backbone models and four benchmark suites with 26 performance and efficiency metrics. Its literature audit of 52 memory systems (2023-2026) finds 62% evaluate only on LoCoMo/LongMemEval and just 21% report any efficiency metric. Finds no universal winner, that wide retrieval helps factual QA but hurts sequential decision-making, and that substrate rankings flip with history length and backbone, motivating substrate routing. Supports treating capability and cost as variables but has no evolution or selection of practices.

papers.title: Hidden in Memory: Sleeper Memory Poisoning in LLM Agents
papers.authors: Sidharth Pulipaka, Stanislau Hlebik, Leonidas Raghav, Sahar Abdelnabi, Vyas Raina, Ivaxi Sheth, Mario Fritz
papers.summary: A black-box external-content adversary (web page, document, email, repo) causes the assistant to write a fabricated memory about the user that lies dormant and resurfaces in later unrelated conversations; success is decomposed into injection, retrieval and adversarial-usage rates under tool-based and external-manager (Mem0-style) memory regimes. An actor-critic loop finds transferable templates: injection rates of 99.8% (GPT-5.5), 99.4% (GPT-5.4), 95.0% (Kimi-K2.6), 88.6% (Gemini-3.1) and 64.2% (Sonnet-4.6, most robust) versus about 3-4% for a naive baseline; goal-adjacent queries retrieve poisoned memories 90-95% of the time; 24/25 manual reproductions on production ChatGPT and Claude. Prompt hardening is brittle under adaptive attack (Kimi 6.2% to 64.6%), while activation probes exceed 0.95 AUROC. Relevant to the proposal's ingestion of neighbour-suggested excerpts.

papers.title: Human-Inspired Memory Architecture for LLM Agents
papers.authors: Doga Kerestecioglu, Alexei Robsky, Clemens Vasters, Anshu Kiran Sharma, Yitzhak Kesselman (Microsoft)
papers.summary: Abstract fetched from microsoft.com: a biologically grounded architecture with six mechanisms, sleep-phase consolidation, interference-based forgetting, engram maturation, reconsolidation upon retrieval, entity knowledge graphs and hybrid multi-cue retrieval, each targeting a failure mode of naive accumulation, plus a synthetic calibration method that sets all thresholds without benchmark exposure. On a 13K-issue / 120K-event VSCode dataset deduplication-based consolidation reaches 97.2% retention precision with 58% store reduction (+21.8 pp); on a streaming LongMemEval evaluation (475 sessions) it reaches 70.1% vs 71.2% for raw retrieval at a 200K budget with a +13.3 pp preference-recall gain at small scale. A fixed, hand-designed consolidation practice; nothing evolves it.
papers.selection_signal: other (synthetically calibrated thresholds; evaluated by labelled benchmarks)

papers.title: HyperAgents: Self-referential self-improving agents that can optimize for any computable task (DGM-H)
papers.authors: Jenny Zhang, Bingchen Zhao, Wannan Yang, Jakob Foerster, Jeff Clune, Minqi Jiang, Sam Devlin, Tatiana Shavrina
papers.summary: Extends the Darwin Gödel Machine by folding the task agent and the meta agent into one editable program so that the meta-level modification procedure itself is modifiable ('metacognitive self-modification'), removing DGM's dependence on coding-domain alignment. Reports that DGM-H improves over time, beats non-self-improving and prior self-improving baselines, and that meta-level improvements transfer across domains and accumulate across runs. Same profile as DGM: generational archive, readable code, benchmark selection, no society or economy.

papers.title: Increasing intelligence in AI agents can worsen collective outcomes
papers.authors: Neil F. Johnson (George Washington University)
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (2603.12129); companion 'Three AI-agents walk into a bar' (2602.23093, Johnson & Mori)
papers.summary: Studies populations of AI agents competing for finite shared capacity with four independently toggled variables: model diversity, individual reinforcement learning, spontaneous tribe formation, and resource scarcity. Under scarcity, model diversity and RL increase dangerous system overload while tribe formation reduces it; under abundance overload goes to near zero; the crossover is set by the capacity-to-population ratio. The companion paper finds LLM agents often do worse than coin flipping at a fixed-capacity request game and that more capable agents increase systemic failure. INFORMS: capability and scarcity as crossed manipulated variables in an agent population already exist, with a 'more capable is worse' result; no memory, text or inheritance.

papers.title: LongMemEval-V2: Evaluating Long-Term Agent Memory Toward Experienced Colleagues
papers.authors: Di Wu, Ji, Kawatkar, Kwan, Gu, Peng, Kai-Wei Chang (UCLA)
papers.venue: arXiv 2605.12493 (May 2026); listed on ICML 2026 virtual site
papers.summary: 451 manually curated questions over haystacks of up to 500 multimodal web-agent trajectories (25M-115M tokens) in web and enterprise environments, probing five abilities: static state recall, dynamic state tracking, workflow knowledge, environment gotchas and premise awareness. Frontier LLMs without trajectory evidence reach at most 14.1%. Proposes AgentRunbook-R (RAG with dedicated memory pools) and AgentRunbook-C (a coding agent that maintains file-based runbooks, manifests and inspection tools); coding-agent memory beats RAG by ~15 points at 5-7x query latency, and the leaderboard scores entries by LAFS gain over an accuracy-latency frontier. Relevant because the file-manipulating runbook is the nearest benchmark analogue to a markdown vault maintained by the agent, scored jointly on accuracy and cost.

papers.title: MAPLE-Guard: Memory-Aware Link Enforcement Against Memory-Link Poisoning in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.authors: Wenjun Xiong, Yijin Zhou, Jiaqian Wang, Shangding Gu, Bo Tang, Zhiyu Li, Feiyu Xiong, Ying Wen, Muning Wen
papers.summary: Models the memory lifecycle in LLM multi-agent systems as four guarded transitions, write, retrieval, promotion from private to shared memory, and cross-agent reuse, plus outcome updates, and defends each link against poisoned memories that are written once, persist, enter shared state and affect a different agent in a later task. Evaluated with Qwen3.5-122B-A10B over star, chain and tree topologies against MINJA, MemoryGraft, AgentPoison, PromptInject and ToolAttack; reports ASR@3 reductions such as 51.4% to 0.3% (MMLU/MINJA) and 38.2% to 0.9% (LongMemEval/MemoryGraft) while raising memory-dependent success rates. The private-to-shared promotion and cross-agent reuse links are precisely the proposal's social transmission channel, here studied as an attack surface rather than a cultural one.

papers.title: Memory Poisoning Attack and Defense on Memory Based LLM-Agents
papers.authors: Balachandra Devarangadi Sunil and five co-authors
papers.summary: Re-evaluates MINJA under realistic conditions on EHR agents with MIMIC-III data (GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.0-Flash, Llama-3.1-8B), varying initial memory state, number of indication prompts and retrieval parameters; finds that pre-existing legitimate memories dramatically reduce attack effectiveness. Proposes two defenses: composite trust-scored input/output moderation and memory sanitization via trust-aware retrieval with temporal decay and pattern filtering, noting that threshold calibration is fragile. Relevant as evidence that a crowded, legitimately accumulated vault is itself protective, and that decay-based retention is a plausible governance primitive.

papers.title: MemoryArena: Benchmarking Agent Memory in Interdependent Multi-Session Agentic Tasks
papers.authors: Zexue He, Yu Wang, Churan Zhi, Yuanzhe Hu, Tzu-Ping Chen, Lang Yin, Ze Chen, Tong Arthur Wu, Siru Ouyang, Zihan Wang, Jiaxin Pei, Julian McAuley, Yejin Choi, Sandy Pentland
papers.summary: Human-crafted agentic tasks with explicitly interdependent subtasks (4,850 subtasks across web shopping navigation, preference-constrained travel planning, progressive web search and sequential formal reasoning) in which the agent must learn from earlier actions and feedback, store it, and reuse it later. Supports long-context, Letta, Mirix, Mem0, ReasoningBank, BM25, embedding RAG, GraphRAG and MemoRAG backends. Headline finding: agents near ceiling on LoCoMo achieve low success here, so recall benchmarks do not predict memory-guided action. Memory accumulates from environment feedback within one agent; no selection among memory practices.

papers.title: MindMemOS: A Portable and Self-Evolving Memory Operating Layer for AI Agents
papers.authors: MindMemOS team (mindscale-noah)
papers.summary: An open-source memory operating layer that persists user profiles, project facts, tool experience and skill candidates as portable assets shared or transferred across different agent frameworks (OpenClaw, Hermes, Claude Code, OpenHands). Self-evolution comes from schema learning (learning frequent memory patterns), 'dreaming' (offline consolidation) and feedback integration that optimises add/search workflows; a Memory-Skills loop distils experience memories into skill candidates whose execution results and failures flow back into memory. Relevant as a system where memory *practice* (schemas, add/search workflow) adapts from feedback and memories are shared across agents, but adaptation is engineering-driven with no selection or inheritance; the paper's experiments were not visible in fetched sources.

papers.title: Multi-LLM Systems Exhibit Robust Semantic Collapse
papers.authors: not recovered
papers.summary: Studies whether multi-LLM systems that feed their own outputs back in closed loops can keep producing novel, diverse content, running up to 1,000 rounds with GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3 and Phi-4 (three replicates each, plus further models for interventions). Diversity is measured as cumulative unique unigrams, cosine distance from the initial window, and cross-run pairwise dissimilarity; the reported conclusion is a robust 'semantic collapse' in which outputs converge in meaning even when wording varies. INFORMS: a nightly LLM rewrite of memory vaults and policy files is exactly such a closed loop, so the proposal needs selection and variation strong enough to counter this attractor; the paper has no agents, selection or economy.

papers.title: OEP: Poisoning Self-Evolving LLM Agents via Locally Correct but Non-Transferable Experiences
papers.authors: Kaixiang Wang, Jiong Lou, Zhaojiacheng Zhou, Jie Li (Shanghai Jiao Tong University)
papers.summary: Obsessive Experience Poisoning is a low-privilege black-box attack needing no control over the system prompt or memory store: the attacker feeds edge-case tasks pairing a locally valid solution, a non-transferable method and severe hypothetical consequences, biasing the agent's reflection toward over-cautious, over-generalised high-priority rules. Exploits the fact that agents over-trust self-generated reflections during memory consolidation; reports >50% ASR on GPT-4o agents and outperforms prior attacks under LLM-auditing defenses because no entry is overtly malicious. Targets exactly the consolidation step (nightly reflection writing rules into a policy file) that the proposal relies on.

papers.title: On Safety Risks in Experience-Driven Self-Evolving Agents
papers.authors: Weixiang Zhao and colleagues
papers.summary: Studies agents that accumulate experience in web and embodied environments and finds that experience gathered solely from benign tasks still compromises safety in high-risk scenarios, because accumulated experience is execution-oriented and reinforces acting over refusing. When both benign and harmful tasks are seen, refusal-related experience limits the decline but induces over-refusal, a safety-utility trade-off. Informs the proposal's no-adversary baseline: an economy that rewards action will select for execution-biased practices even without poisoning.

papers.title: Rethinking Memory as Continuously Evolving Connectivity (FluxMem)
papers.authors: Jizhan Fang, Buqiang Xu, Zhixian Wang, Haoliang Cao, Xinle Deng et al. (Zhejiang University, Alibaba, MemTensor, Tongji)
papers.venue: arXiv 2605.28773 (May 2026; under review at EMNLP 2026 per LightMem README)
papers.summary: Models memory as a heterogeneous graph with semantic, episodic and procedural nodes linked by typed edges (Ground, Distill, StepLink) and evolves its topology in three stages: online initial connection formation per step, online feedback-driven refinement that attributes failures and repairs the graph (expanding missing links, pruning interference, reshaping granularity), and offline periodic consolidation that clusters trajectories and distils procedural skills until a PEMS maturity metric converges. Reports consistent SOTA on LoCoMo, Mind2Web and GAIA versus static and meta-evolving baselines, shipped inside zjunlp/LightMem. An adjacent consolidation mechanism: the evolving unit is memory structure for one agent, with task failure as the signal.

papers.title: Retrieval-Driven Memory Reconsolidation for Long-Term LLM Agents (REALM)
papers.authors: Yuanyi Song and nine co-authors (names beyond first author not retrievable)
papers.summary: Argues existing memory systems update only on arrival and treat retrieval as the endpoint of memory access; REALM instead models long-term memory as a continual lifecycle: memories are organised into a heterogeneous cognitive graph, evidence is retrieved via adaptively composed graph-search atoms, and memories are reconsolidated based on retrieval feedback, echoing the neuroscience notion that recalled memories become labile. Reports 75.97% on LoCoMo and 65.11% on LongMemEval (+7.17 / +1.31 over strongest baselines) with ablations showing removal of reconsolidation degrades both. Retrieval outcomes reshape memory structure, which is adjacent to the proposal's 'practice revised from use' idea but single-agent and unselected.
papers.evolving_unit: memory structure (cognitive graph reorganised by retrieval feedback)

papers.title: SCM: Sleep-Consolidated Memory with Algorithmic Forgetting for Large Language Models
papers.authors: single author; name not retrievable from accessible sources
papers.summary: A five-component LLM memory architecture: capacity-limited working memory, four-dimensional importance tagging of semantic concepts, offline sleep cycles with separate NREM and REM consolidation stages, deliberate value-based forgetting, and a self-model for introspection. Self-reported results on an eight-test suite: perfect recall over ten-turn conversations, 90.9% memory-noise reduction via adaptive forgetting, sub-millisecond retrieval at hundreds of concepts. Single-agent, heuristic importance scores, no external selection, no peer review found.
papers.evolving_unit: memory content (consolidated concepts) and importance scores
papers.selection_signal: other (internal importance/value heuristics; no external judge)
papers.readable_trace: unknown (semantic concept store; format not confirmed)

papers.title: SkillJack: Persistent Skill Backdoors in Self-Evolving Agents
papers.authors: Tencent Zhuque Lab (individual names not retrieved)
papers.summary: Targets the experience-to-skill pipeline rather than retrieval: a poisoned trajectory is distilled into the agent's reusable skill library, exhibiting 'sanitization whitewashing' (intent hidden during extraction), 'cross-layer promotion' (ephemeral experience becomes lasting capability) and 'persistence isolation' (payload outlives its source records). On SkillX and Anything2Skill with 150 trajectories, the safety check flagged 98.5% of raw poisoned trajectories but only 11.4% of distilled skills; ASR was 56.2% and 89.2%, and 80% of skill-mediated attacks survived deletion of the source records. Shows that provenance must be carried through consolidation, which matters for any inherited, re-summarised practice file.

papers.title: STATE-Bench: Stateful Task Agent Evaluation Benchmark
papers.authors: Microsoft (open-source release, no paper author list)
papers.venue: Open-source release, Microsoft Open Source blog, May 2026 (no peer-reviewed paper found)
papers.summary: 450 synthetic enterprise tasks (150 each in travel, customer support, shopping) with sandboxed databases, domain tools, simulated users and deterministic final-state assertions; metrics are pass@1, pass^5 consistency, an LLM-judged UX score and cost per task in dollars. The Agent Learning Track adds training trajectories and a retrieval hook for 'reusable learnings' (memories, skills or prompt optimisations), so the benchmark is memory-agnostic and scores whether agents improve with experience; Microsoft reports ~5% gains from procedural memory. Relevant as a cost-per-task harness in which the evolving artifact can be a text playbook, but selection is by task metric and there is no economy or population.

papers.title: The Memory Trust Gap: Capability-Dependent Failures in Persistent-Memory Agents
papers.authors: Not retrieved
papers.summary: Proposes a frozen, SHA-256-pinned two-suite benchmark (a Benefit suite where the stored fact is required, and a Safety suite where an authoritative tool always holds the correct value) and evaluates a Qwen3 model-size series plus Llama-Instruct, RGB and MisBench. Finds the failure is over-trust rather than confusion: reliance on stale stored values stays about 1.0 across sizes, but net harm from memory is capability-gated, appearing only once the model is accurate enough for the stale value to cost it, and the memory feature that triggers failure shifts with scale. Mitigation is also capability-dependent: metadata helps capable models while only pre-resolution restores accuracy for small ones. One of the very few papers treating model capability as an explicit factor in memory behaviour; it predicts capability-by-memory interactions the proposal must control for.

papers.title: The Role of Social Learning and Collective Norm Formation in Fostering Cooperation in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
papers.authors: Prateek Gupta, Qiankun Zhong, Hiromu Yakura, Thomas Eisenmann, Iyad Rahwan (MPI for Human Development)
papers.summary: Common-pool-resource simulation with no explicit reward function in which agents adopt strategies and beliefs from more successful peers (social learning), punish via Ostrom-style norms, and individually learn from environmental feedback on harvesting, monitoring and punishing. Reproduces key human-behaviour findings, then tests rich/scarce x altruistic/selfish conditions and compares societies built from different LLMs, finding systematic model differences in sustaining cooperation and norm formation. Close to the 'neighbours suggest practices' mechanism with capability as a factor, but no inheritance, no mortality and no memory file.
papers.evolving_unit: prompt/playbook (strategies and beliefs copied from successful peers)

papers.title: The Yerkes-Dodson Curve for AI Agents: Optimal Environmental Pressure for Emergent Complexity in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
papers.authors: Ivan Pasichnyk (WeLabelData Inc.)
papers.summary: A 'Survival Arena' grid-world with 16 Claude 3.5 Sonnet agents over 60 turns choosing among gathering, movement, combat, trade and reproduction; pressure is varied via an upkeep cost (scarcity) and a sexual-selection reproduction mechanic. Trades follow an inverted U, peaking at 29 under medium upkeep (=5) versus 8-12 at low or extreme pressure; under extreme pressure the behavioural repertoire collapses to movement-only within 5-12 turns; sexual selection eliminates inter-agent aggression and elicits communication absent under survival pressure. INFORMS: the proposal should sweep scarcity rather than pick one level, since too much selection pressure collapses behaviour before any practice can be selected; single model, no inheritance of practices.

papers.title: Total Recall at What Cost? Benchmarking the Serving Cost of Agentic Memory Systems
papers.authors: Natchanon Pollertlam, Witchayut Kornsuwannawit (Bricks Technology)
papers.summary: Measures billable serving cost of Mem0, Hindsight and Mastra Observational Memory against a rolling-window and a full-transcript baseline across two backbones and conversations up to 400 turns, pairing cost with accuracy on 665 LoCoMo questions to get cost-per-correct-answer. A regression fitted on the baselines mispredicts memory-system cost by 18-69% because internal memory behaviour drives the bill; break-even versus full replay ranges from tens of turns to never within 400 turns; accuracy spans 21-54% and backbone choice affects cost as much as memory system choice. An economy-of-memory measurement without any agent facing the bill.

papers.title: What Deserves Memory: Adaptive Memory Distillation for LLM Agents (Nemori)
papers.authors: Wenquan Ma et al. (Fudan University, Shanda Group, Beihang University, Shanghai Univ. of Finance and Economics)
papers.venue: ACL 2026 long paper, pp. 34789-34812 (earlier arXiv 2508.03341, Aug 2025)
papers.summary: Replaces heuristic importance scores with a prediction-error criterion drawn from predictive coding: observations the agent fails to predict from existing knowledge are what gets retained. Two modules: segment raw interaction into topic-coherent episodic narratives (Event Segmentation Theory) and distil durable semantic insights where predictions break down; the authors map this two-module design onto Complementary Learning Systems. Reports strong gains over prior systems on LoCoMo and LongMemEval, especially at longer contexts, with reduced storage; README confirms a self-organising memory substrate that distils durable knowledge from episodes. A principled 'what to keep' rule, but fixed rather than evolved.
papers.evolving_unit: memory content (episodes and distilled semantic knowledge)
papers.selection_signal: other (prediction error gates retention; benchmarks for evaluation)

papers.title: What to Keep, What to Forget: A Rate-Distortion View of Memory Compaction in LLMs and Agents
papers.authors: Ashwin Gerard Colaco, Nada Lahjouji (UC Irvine)
papers.summary: Unifies KV-cache eviction, prompt pruning/distillation, bounded architectural state and agent memory consolidation as a single rate-distortion decision: which context-derived information to keep, how faithfully, under a resource budget, while preserving task performance. Proposes a compaction objective, a layer-agnostic lower bound and a seven-axis taxonomy, and argues most methods decide by attention magnitude or recency, discarding irreversibly before the query is known. Notes that repeated compaction performed by agents is almost never measured and proposes a benchmark plus a small reference experiment. Useful theory for a memory-policy fitness landscape; no evolution or selection of policies.
papers.selection_signal: labelled task metric (distortion measured against task performance)
papers.readable_trace: unknown (framework spans KV cache and text memory)

papers.title: When Does Memory Help? A Cost-Aware Evaluation of Long-Term Memory in Tool-Using LLM Agents (MERIT)
papers.authors: Shweta Mishra, Shashank Mishra (independent)
papers.summary: MERIT (Memory Evaluation for Realistic Instrumented Tasks) runs episodic tool-use tasks in three seeded SQLite worlds (commerce support, IT ops, personal assistant) with a leak-verified difficulty ladder (single-fact, multi-fact, updated-fact), injected stale/contradictory/distractor memories, six memory conditions (none, full replay, embedding retrieval, LLM summarisation, structured fact store, hybrid) and full token/dollar/wall-time metering of every memory call (23,440 episodes, ~$44). Memory lifts dependent-task success from 0 to 0.55-1.00, but embedding retrieval collapses on updated facts and is unstable across agent models and seeds, agents ignore ~45-50% of correctly retrieved facts, swapping implementation moves success by up to 60-100 points, and full replay is never the most economical (best condition yields 2.7-3.9x marginal utility per dollar, the CAMU metric). Directly relevant as a template for pricing memory operations and for showing that capability (gpt-4.1-mini vs GPT-4.1 vs Claude Haiku 4.5) changes which memory design wins; it does not evolve or select memory practices.

papers.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Self-Evolving AI Agents: A New Paradigm Bridging Foundation Models and Lifelong Agentic Systems
papers.authors: Jinyuan Fang, Yanwen Peng, Xi Zhang, Yingxu Wang, Xinhao Yi, Guibin Zhang, et al.
papers.summary: Surveys single-agent optimisation (behaviour, prompt optimisation incl. evolutionary methods such as EvoPrompt/Promptbreeder/GEPA, memory optimisation, tool optimisation), multi-agent optimisation (automatic construction, workflow evolution, decentralised evolutionary coordination e.g. AgentNet), domain-specific systems, and evaluation including safety/alignment benchmarks for lifelong agents. Explicitly groups evolutionary coding agents (AlphaEvolve, OpenEvolve, Darwin Goedel Machine). Useful for positioning and for its safety section; it lists memory optimisation and evolutionary methods as separate lines, with no entry combining them under ecological selection.

papers.title: A Self-Improving Coding Agent (SICA)
papers.authors: Maxime Robeyns, Martin Szummer, Laurence Aitchison
